sections.title: Taxonomy and names
sections.text: Species Fungorum, through Index Fungorum, currently accepts Collybia nuda (Bull.) Z.M. He & Zhu L. Yang, published as a new combination in 2023. Its basionym is Agaricus nudus Bull. (1790). Lepista nuda and Clitocybe nuda are historical combinations still widely used in field guides and edibility lists; Tricholoma nudum is another synonym. Common names include wood blewit and blewit.

sections.title: Cap and gills
sections.text: The cap is usually 4–14 cm across, occasionally reaching 18 cm. It starts convex with an inrolled margin, then flattens and may become irregular, wavy or broadly umbonate. Its smooth surface is violet to blue-violet when young and fresh, then often fades toward brown, buff or tan; it can feel lubricous in damp weather but is not truly viscid. The gills are close to crowded and fairly broad, lilac to pale violet, then pinkish buff or brownish with age. They are adnate to notched, sometimes slightly decurrent. The spore deposit is dull pink to pinkish buff.

sections.title: Stem, flesh and smell
sections.text: The stout stem is about 2.5–10 cm tall and 1–3 cm wide. It is solid, equal or widened into a club-shaped base, lilac to pale violet and often browning with age; whitish fibrils may streak its surface, and lilac mycelium can surround the base. There is no ring or cortina. The thick, pliant flesh is lilac to lilac-buff, then fades toward whitish. The smell is faint and pleasantly fruity or fragrant; a strong anise smell is not a dependable identifying feature.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This saprotroph decomposes leaf litter and other plant debris. It grows singly, in groups, arcs or rings in broadleaf and conifer woods, as well as gardens, compost and other places rich in organic matter. Fruiting is mainly in autumn and may extend from late summer into early winter depending on climate. It can tolerate cold and frost, but the first frost is not a diagnostic feature.

traits: Smooth cap 4–14 cm across, sometimes 18 cm, violet to blue-violet when young, often fading to buff or brown; margin initially inrolled.
Close to crowded gills, lilac then pinkish buff to brownish, attached or notched at the stem; dull pink to pinkish-buff spore deposit.
Stout, solid stem, lilac then browning, often widened at the base and streaked with whitish fibrils; no ring or cortina.
Thick, pliant flesh, lilac then fading; faint, pleasant fruity fragrance, with no consistent anise note.
Saprotroph of leaf litter and plant debris in broadleaf or conifer woods, gardens and compost; sometimes in arcs or rings.
Fruits mainly in autumn, sometimes into early winter; cold tolerance varies and is not enough to identify it.
safetyNote: The DGfM (Germany) and VAPKO (Switzerland) lists include Lepista nuda among species regarded or recommended as edible; these lists use the older name and do not verify a specimen's identity. Blewits should be thoroughly cooked and may cause intolerance in some people. Violet Cortinarius species can look similar: a cortina and rusty-brown spore deposit are useful clues, but no single feature guarantees identification. This page cannot determine whether a wild collection is safe to eat.
